hints: Recall Malus law: transmitted intensity depends on angle between incident polarisation and transmission axis, with maximum when aligned and zero when perpendicular.
Identify the angles for full transmission and for extinction in one full $360^{\circ}$ rotation, then join them with a smooth $\cos^2$ shaped curve.
teacher_walkthrough: Malus law for polarised light is $$I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta$$ where $\theta$ is angle between incident polarisation direction and transmission axis.
At $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ the transmission axis is vertical and parallel to incident polarisation, so $$I = I_0$$ which is the maximum value.
At $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ the transmission axis is horizontal and perpendicular to incident polarisation, so $$I = I_0 \cos^2 90^{\circ} = 0$$.
The pattern repeats with period $180^{\circ}$ because $\cos^2(\theta + 180^{\circ}) = \cos^2 \theta$. So maxima at $0^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, $360^{\circ}$ and zeros at $90^{\circ}$, $270^{\circ}$.
Sketch a smooth curve starting at maximum, falling to zero at $90^{\circ}$, rising to maximum at $180^{\circ}$, falling to zero at $270^{\circ}$, rising to maximum at $360^{\circ}$.
walkthrough: M1: maxima at 0, 180, 360 degrees and zero at 90, 270 degrees
A1: smooth cos-squared shaped curve through those points
common_pitfalls: Drawing a straight line zigzag between maxima and minima instead of a smooth curved variation.
Showing only one maximum in 360 degrees, confusing intensity period with 360 degrees instead of 180 degrees.

hints: Apply Malus law $I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta$ with $I_0 = 7.6\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}$ and $I = 4.2\,\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}$.
Rearrange to $\cos^2 \theta = I/I_0$, then take square root and inverse cosine to find $\theta$ in degrees.
common_pitfalls: Using $I = I_0 \cos \theta$ without squaring, giving an incorrect smaller angle.
Leaving calculator in radian mode and reporting $\theta$ in radians or an incorrect degree value.

hints: Recall the condition for diffraction: what type of obstacle or opening must the wave meet.
Recall what happens to the direction of the wave after that encounter, especially beyond the straight through path.
teacher_walkthrough: Diffraction is defined by two required ideas.
A wave encounters an aperture, slit, gap or an edge or obstacle of size comparable to wavelength.
After passing, the wave spreads out from the aperture or around the edge into the region of geometrical shadow.
walkthrough: B1: wave passes through an aperture or past an edge
B1: wave spreads into geometrical shadow
common_pitfalls: Confusing diffraction with interference or polarisation, for example stating waves overlap or are filtered.
Omitting the spreading idea and stating only that the wave bends or passes through, which is insufficient for both marks.

hints: Use the diffraction grating equation $d \sin \theta = n \lambda$ with order $n = 3$, $\lambda = 4.3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ and $\theta = 68^{\circ}$.
Rearrange to $d = n\lambda / \sin \theta$ and evaluate $\sin 68^{\circ}$ before dividing.
teacher_walkthrough: Diffraction grating condition for a maximum is $$d \sin \theta = n \lambda$$
walkthrough: C1: n lambda = d sin theta
common_pitfalls: Using $\theta$ in radians or using $\sin \theta$ incorrectly, for example using $\cos \theta$.
Confusing line spacing $d$ with number of lines per metre $N$, and giving $1/d$ as the answer.

hints: For the same $d$ and same $\theta = 68^{\circ}$, the product $d \sin \theta$ is fixed, so $n\lambda$ must be constant for any overlapping maximum.
Set $n\lambda = 3 \times 4.3 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ and test integer orders $n = 1, 2, 4$ to find a $\lambda$ in the visible range $4.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ to $7.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$.
teacher_walkthrough: For a fixed grating and fixed angle, $$d \sin \theta = n \lambda = \text{constant}$$
For a different order $n$ at same angle: $$\lambda = \frac{1.29 \times 10^{-6}}{n}$$

This lies in visible red light. Other orders give $n=1$ with $1.29 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}$ in infrared and $n=4$ with $3.2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ in ultraviolet, so $n=2$ is the required visible overlap.
walkthrough: C1: d sin68 = 2 x lambda or 3 x 4.3 x 10^-7 = 2 x lambda
common_pitfalls: Assuming only one wavelength can diffract to a given angle and not realising different orders can overlap.
Calculating a wavelength outside the visible spectrum, for example using $n=1$ or $n=4$, without checking $4.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$ to $7.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}$.
